title: Voice prompting — four wording and behaviour decisions before the build

steps.surface: Message box → while the mic listens
steps.path: You approved (V-6): the newest two words show grey until they settle, then turn solid. Building it, we measured the real speech engine and found that is not true of it — so this is a promise we cannot keep as written, and the choice is yours
steps.headline: Solid text can still change. Should more of it stay grey, or should we change what grey means?

options.label: Grey everything since your last full stop (recommended)
options.summary: What we found: the engine keeps re-hearing your whole sentence, so it adds and moves commas in words you have already seen turn solid. Reading the sample sentence aloud, a comma appeared after a word three places back, in black text. With this option, everything you have said since your last full stop stays grey, and turns solid the moment you finish a sentence. Pro: black text then never changes, which is what you approved. Con: while you are mid-sentence a lot of the box is grey, and if you talk for a long time without a full stop it is nearly all grey.
options.cost: The grey boundary follows sentence endings instead of a word count.

options.label: Keep two grey words, and accept that commas can appear in black text
options.summary: The box looks calmer and mostly solid while you talk, exactly as you saw it on the deck, but a comma or full stop can quietly appear or move in a line you already read as finished. The words themselves almost never change; it is the punctuation that moves. Pro: closest to what you approved and the least visual noise. Con: something changes in front of you without being marked as unfinished.
options.cost: Nothing changes in the build; the promise on the acceptance deck is reworded.

options.label: Grey the last six words instead of two
options.summary: A middle setting: a wider grey tail that covers most of what we measured moving, without going all the way to sentence boundaries. Pro: less grey than option A, catches most changes. Con: it is a guess — we measured changes three words back on a clean recording, and hesitant speech gives the engine more to revise, so some will still slip into black.
options.cost: One number changes; the risk does not fully go away.

steps.path: You approved the card reading 'One-time download: 464 MB'. That number was the speech model alone, and rounded the way we compute it, not the way your computer reports it. The real first-time download also includes the small engine that runs the model
steps.headline: What size should the first-run card promise?

options.label: The true total, about 500 MB (recommended)
options.summary: The card says 'One-time download: about 500 MB'. This is everything that is actually fetched the first time: the speech model plus the engine that runs it. Pro: nobody watches a download run past the number they were promised, which reads as broken. Con: a bigger number than you approved, which may put some people off before they try it.

options.label: Keep 464 MB
options.summary: The card keeps the number you approved. Pro: the smallest number that is defensible about the model itself. Con: a user watching their downloads sees roughly 500 MB arrive against a 464 MB promise, and the difference is visible.
options.cost: Nothing; the promise is knowingly under the real figure.

steps.path: The engine we chose understands English and 24 other European languages, and nothing else. Someone dictating in Japanese or Arabic would download half a gigabyte and get nonsense
steps.headline: Should the first-run card say which languages the mic understands?

options.label: Yes, one short line (recommended)
options.summary: The card gains: 'Understands English and 24 other European languages.' Pro: someone it will not work for finds out before a 500 MB download instead of after. Con: a third line on a card you approved with two, and a reminder of a limit most of your users will never hit.

options.label: No, keep the card as approved
options.summary: The card stays exactly as you signed it off. Pro: shortest card, no extra reading for the many people it works for. Con: a speaker of an unsupported language downloads it, tries it, gets nonsense, and has no explanation.
options.cost: Nothing now; likely a support question later.

steps.surface: Message box → the card, right after the download bar fills
steps.path: The download arrives as one compressed file that then has to be expanded, which takes tens of seconds on a slow machine. On the card you approved, the bar would sit full and still for that whole time, which reads as stuck
steps.headline: What should the card show while the download is being unpacked?

options.label: 'Unpacking…' with a moving bar (recommended)
options.summary: When the download finishes the card's label changes to 'Unpacking…' and the bar keeps moving without showing a percentage, because there is no reliable one to show. Pro: obviously still working, and the mic becomes ready the moment it ends. Con: a third state on the card, and a bar that moves without meaning a measured amount.
options.cost: One more state on the card.

options.label: 'Almost ready…' with a moving bar
options.summary: The same thing in plainer words, saying nothing about what is happening under the hood. Pro: nobody has to know what unpacking is. Con: vaguer, and if it takes a minute on an old laptop 'almost' starts to feel untrue.
